screens.title: Navigating the Unity Editor for Artists
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we’ll make the Unity Editor feel like your studio. You will learn what each core window does, how to move confidently through a 3D scene, and how to arrange the workspace so your art work stays visible and accessible. Artists use the Scene view to place and polish assets, the Game view to check the player’s perspective, the Hierarchy to structure scene objects, the Project window to manage files, and the Inspector to tune properties. I’ll show concrete navigation habits—like orbiting, panning, and using keyboard movement bindings—that save time while modeling and composing. We’ll also practice creating and saving an artist layout so you never lose a comfortable setup. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes—like dumping imports in the project root or ignoring import scale—that lead to confusion later. By the end, you’ll know which window to reach for when you want to reposition a prop, verify materials, or change a texture import setting. Think of this session as building a dependable studio workflow: small navigation habits and a tidy project structure translate to faster iterations and clearer visuals. Ready to set up your artist workspace?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify core editor windows, move efficiently through a 3D scene, create a custom artist layout, and use keyboard shortcuts that speed selection and manipulation. First, you’ll learn to recognize and describe the purpose of the Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector windows so you can pick the right tool for a task. Second, you’ll practice the fundamental navigation operations—panning, zooming, orbiting, and the fly controls—so moving through large scenes becomes quick and precise. Third, you’ll customize and save a layout tailored to visual work, which reduces the time spent resizing and redocking panels. Fourth, you’ll learn common keyboard shortcuts that let you switch between move, rotate, and scale tools and focus on selected objects. Each objective includes a short practice or micro-check to ensure you can perform the action, and you’ll be asked to reflect on a layout that supports your personal pipeline. These skills matter because they reduce context switching, limit errors during importing and placement, and keep your focus on lighting, composition, and material adjustments rather than hunting for windows.

screens.title: Objectives — Practical outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are written to be demonstrable. You should be able to point to a window and state its purpose, perform a set of navigation maneuvers in the Scene view, and adjust import or material properties in the Inspector. For example, after practice you’ll import an FBX model, select it in the Project window, and change its import scale and orientation in the Inspector. You should also be able to select a Directional Light in the Hierarchy, focus it, orbit around it, and confirm how shadows behave in the Game view. Another objective is to create a simple folder structure, move assets into the correct folders, and explain why consistent naming matters for collaboration. Finally, you’ll save a custom layout and recall it on a new project. These are not abstract skills: they are the everyday operations that keep your visual pipeline fast, reproducible, and easy to share with other artists or engineers.

screens.title: Scene View — Your 3D canvas
screens.narratorSegment: The Scene view is the interactive 3D viewport where you arrange and polish your assets. As an artist, you’ll spend the majority of your time here aligning models, placing lights, and previewing materials under scene lighting. Define it as your virtual studio: you can select objects, move them, change their parents, and preview how transformations affect the whole composition. A common practice is to orbit and pan frequently while modeling so you can inspect silhouettes and proportions from multiple angles. For example, select a small vase, press F to focus, then orbit while checking the rim for shading issues. A frequent misconception is that the Game view and Scene view are identical; they are not. Scene view offers editing controls, gizmos, and scene overlays that the Game view hides. Another mistake is relying only on mouse wheel zoom—mixing fly keys with right-button movement gives more precise camera placement in large scenes. Try this: pick a light, focus on it, move around using right-click plus WASD for smooth camera flight, and adjust the light until reflections look correct on a nearby model. The takeaway: make Scene view navigation habitual and precise, because fast, controlled viewing prevents small modeling errors from becoming big problems later.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Scene View — Your 3D canvas
Definition

The Scene view is the editable, real-time 3D viewport used for arranging and manipulating GameObjects and visual elements.

Focus (F) to center selected object and reset orbit pivot.
Orbit with right-click; pan with middle mouse; zoom with mouse wheel for quick inspection.
Combine right-click with W/A/S/D and Q/E to fly through large scenes precisely.
Key Takeaway

Make a habit of focusing small objects and using fly controls to inspect for shading and alignment issues.

Practical Example

Select a prop, press F to focus, then orbit to check normals and silhouette from multiple angles. Adjust position and rotation until the composition reads clearly at the camera distance you expect the player to see.

Common mistake
Relying only on Game view for composition; you lose access to editing gizmos and fine placement control.
Pro tip
Use F frequently and orbit slowly to spot texture seams or incorrect pivot placement before you bake lighting.

screens.title: Scene Navigation Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Good camera control in the Scene view is a set of small, repeatable actions. Start with pan: hold the middle mouse button and drag to translate the view parallel to the screen—this is useful when lining up elements without changing perspective. Zoom with the scroll wheel for coarse distance changes; for precision, use focus on an object and then orbit. Orbiting is done with the right mouse button and mouse movement; it rotates the camera around the pivot point. A common, powerful technique is to combine right-button orbit with WASD and Q/E keys: this gives you a smooth fly-through camera that’s invaluable in larger environments where single-click pans feel imprecise. For example, when placing streetlamps across a scene, focus the first lamp, orbit to set angle, then fly forward with W and fine-tune with middle-mouse pans. A misconception is that faster camera movement always speeds work; it can make you miss alignment errors. Practice slow orbits when checking normals or material seams. Finally, learn the F key to focus objects and re-center your pivot. This saves time when scaling or rotating small props and ensures the gizmo handles behave predictably. Try a quick drill: focus, orbit, pan, zoom, and repeat until each movement feels natural and deliberate.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable movement patterns
keyIdea.text: Combine focus, orbit, pan, and fly to inspect, place, and align assets accurately in scenes of any size.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Scene Navigation Controls
Step-by-step camera drill
  1. Pan: Hold middle mouse and drag to shift the view parallel to screen.
  2. Zoom: Use scroll wheel; for fine control, focus first, then zoom.
  3. Orbit: Hold right mouse and move to rotate around pivot.
  4. Fly: Hold right mouse and use W/A/S/D + Q/E to move through scene.
  5. Focus: Press F on a selected object to center pivot and improve orbit precision.
Key Takeaway

Sequence your movements: focus first, orbit slowly, then pan and fine-tune to avoid overshooting small details.

Example Drill

Select a flickering lamp model, press F, orbit to inspect the bulb's rim, fly in with W while holding right mouse to position, then use middle-mouse pan to align against the pole. Repeat until the silhouette is clean from multiple angles.

Common mistake
Zooming aggressively without focusing can change the pivot and make rotations feel slippery.
Pro tip
Set a comfortable mouse sensitivity and practice slow orbits for checking normals and texture seams.

screens.title: Game View — The player’s perspective
screens.narratorSegment: The Game view renders exactly what the player will see, based on the active camera in your scene. For an artist, it is the critical feedback loop: you make changes in the Scene view and verify them in the Game view to confirm composition, camera framing, and material appearance in play conditions. Unlike Scene view, the Game view hides editing gizmos and overlays, and it uses the camera’s projection, resolution, and post-processing settings. For example, your model may look correctly lit in Scene view, but in Game view the camera’s exposure or post-process bloom could alter highlights and color saturation. A common misconception is treating the Game view as purely for programmers; artists must use it to ensure that trims, specular highlights, and camera-driven effects work at the intended resolution. Try this concrete check: set the Game view resolution to the target device, run the Scene view changes, and compare. If a texture looks too shiny in Game view, inspect the material’s Smoothness and Metallic values in the Inspector; the Game view is your final arbiter for how the player will perceive your art. Ultimately, switching frequently between Scene and Game view keeps visual intent aligned with final presentation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Game View — The player’s perspective
What it is

The Game view shows the rendered output from your active camera and reflects resolution, post-processing, and camera settings the player will experience.

Use Game view to test camera framing, exposure, and post-processing effects at target resolution.
Switch sizes: set Game view to the expected device resolution to check readability and composition.
Key Takeaway

Validate every material and lighting change in Game view to ensure it reads properly for players.

Example Scenario

You adjusted a metal material to be more reflective. In Scene view it looked subtle, but in Game view bloom made it dominate the frame. Adjust the material's Smoothness and the post-process settings until highlights match the intended style.

Misconception
Assuming Scene view appearance equals final output; they differ because Game view applies camera and rendering settings.
Check
Always preview in Game view at the target resolution before considering a composition finished.

screens.title: Hierarchy Window — Structure and parenting
screens.narratorSegment: The Hierarchy window lists every GameObject in the active scene and displays parent-child relationships. For artists, using parenting deliberately simplifies complex transformations: moving a parent moves all its children, which is useful for grouped props like a character and its accessories. Define parenting as a way to lock multiple pieces to a single transform operation. For example, a street lamp assembly might have separate child objects for pole, lamp head, and bulb; rotating the pole should keep the lamp head and bulb attached. A common mistake is parenting meshes to each other without considering pivot placement—if the parent's pivot is far from the visible geometry, rotation and scale behavior can become awkward. Use empty GameObjects as organizational parents to provide predictable pivot points. Also keep the Hierarchy tidy: name objects descriptively and use folders or empty containers to group related items. This helps collaboration since other artists or engineers can understand intent at a glance. After organizing, practice: create a parent container, move a group into it, and then move the parent—observe how child transforms follow. The takeaway: good hierarchy design reduces errors and saves time when you need to move or duplicate complex assemblies.

keyIdea.text: Use parent containers and well-placed pivots to make group transforms simple and predictable for complex assemblies.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Hierarchy Window — Structure and parenting
Hierarchy principles
  • Use clear, descriptive names for GameObjects to communicate role in the scene.
  • Group related meshes under an empty GameObject to create predictable pivots.
  • Parent transforms cascade: moving a parent affects all children consistently.
Key Takeaway

Design the Hierarchy for predictable transforms and team readability; use empty parents as pivot anchors.

Example

Create an empty parent named "Bench_Group" and move individual bench planks as children. Rotating or moving "Bench_Group" repositions all planks while preserving local offsets.

Common mistake
Parenting directly to meshes with poor pivot locations, causing unexpected rotations or scales when transforming the parent.
Pro tip
When a predictable pivot is needed, create an empty GameObject at the desired pivot point and make geometry its child.

screens.title: Project Window — Asset management for artists
screens.narratorSegment: The Project window is your asset library: it contains models, textures, materials, and any file in the Unity project. For an artist, a well-organized Project window is essential to maintain speed and avoid duplication. Use clear top-level folders like Models, Textures, Materials, and Scenes. When importing, place assets into the correct folder immediately rather than dumping them in the root. A common mistake is inconsistent naming—different artists might import the same prop under slightly different names and create redundant files. For example, import a rock model into Models/Rocks/LowPoly and place its texture in Textures/Rocks; then create a Material in Materials/Rocks that references those textures. This predictable layout makes it easy to find and reuse assets across scenes. Another practical habit is to use subfolders for LODs, variations, and source files. Finally, remember that moving assets in the Project window can break references if done carelessly; use Unity's move operations rather than moving files outside the editor. The takeaway: a disciplined Project window structure saves time in team projects and makes bulk updates straightforward. Project Window — Asset management for artists means create consistent folders and naming conventions so assets are easy to find, reuse, and update across scenes and teams.. In practical terms, organize imports, naming, and folder structure to keep your project reusable and clear.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Project Window — Asset management
Best practices
  • Create top-level folders: Models, Textures, Materials, Scenes, Prefabs.
  • Place imports immediately in the appropriate folder to avoid clutter.
  • Use descriptive and consistent naming conventions for assets and folders.
Why it matters

Clear structure reduces duplicate imports and saves time when assembling scenes or collaborating with others.

Example organization
Models/Rocks/LowPoly/Rock_A.fbx
Textures/Rocks/Rock_A_Diffuse.png
Materials/Rocks/Rock_A_Mat
Common mistake
Dropping all imports in the project root and relying on search later; this becomes unmanageable quickly.
Pro tip
Create a simple README in top folders documenting naming conventions and LOD rules for your team.

screens.title: Inspector Window — Adjusting properties precisely
screens.narratorSegment: The Inspector is the context-sensitive control panel that shows properties for the currently selected GameObject or asset. When you select a model in the Project window, the Inspector reveals import settings like scale, normals, and mesh compression. Selecting a GameObject shows Transform, Mesh Renderer, Materials, and any attached components. For artists, the Inspector is the place to fine-tune material parameters—like Metallic and Smoothness—adjust light intensity or color, and change camera settings such as field of view. A useful example: import a character model and set Import Scale to match your scene, then inspect normals and axis orientation. Another example is selecting a material and tweaking its Smoothness until reflections look correct in both Scene and Game views. A misconception is that the Inspector is only for programmers; it is where artists make critical aesthetic adjustments. Remember to select the asset in the Project window to edit import settings, not just the instance in the scene. The takeaway: learn which Inspector panels control visual properties you care about and make small, iterative changes while checking the Game view to validate results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Inspector Window — Adjusting properties
Inspector essentials
  • Edit import settings by selecting an asset in the Project window.
  • Tune material parameters like Metallic and Smoothness to control reflections.
  • Adjust transforms, light intensity, and camera FOV directly on selected GameObjects.
Key Takeaway

Use the Inspector to iterate quickly: make a small change, then check the Game view to validate the visible result.

Concrete example

Select a texture in the Project window and change its Compression or Max Size in the Inspector to balance quality and memory. Then assign it to a material and check lighting response in the Game view.

Common mistake
Editing a scene instance’s property when the underlying asset needs change. To alter import settings, select the asset in the Project window.
Pro tip
Use the Inspector search box to find a specific component quickly on complex GameObjects.

screens.title: Customize and Save an Artist Layout
screens.narratorSegment: Customizing the editor layout tailors the workspace to your art tasks and reduces wasted time resizing or hunting for tabs. Begin by dragging the Game tab next to the Scene tab to create a split view so you can edit and preview simultaneously. Move the Project window to the bottom to span full width—this helps when browsing assets or dragging textures onto materials. Keep the Hierarchy on the left and Inspector on the right for quick selection and property editing. Once you have a comfortable arrangement, save it via Window then Layouts then Save Layout and give it a clear name like Artist Layout. A concrete example: place Scene on the left two-thirds, Game on the right third, Project across the bottom, and Inspector narrow on the right. A common misconception is that one layout fits every task; instead, save multiple layouts for modeling, lighting, and UI work. The practical benefit is faster context switching: when you switch tasks, recalling a layout instantly repositions windows and restores your muscle memory. Try this workflow: create the split view, adjust sizes to emphasize Scene view, save the layout, then reopen a new project and load your saved layout to confirm it persists. The takeaway: saved layouts keep your studio consistent and reproducible across projects.

A common misconception is that one layout fits every task; instead, save multiple layouts for modeling, lighting, and UI work. The practical benefit is faster context switching: when you switch tasks, recalling a layout instantly repositions windows and restores your muscle memory. Try this workflow: create the split view, adjust sizes to emphasize Scene view, save the layout, then reopen a new project and load your saved layout to confirm it persists. screens.title: Tools and Shortcuts
screens.narratorSegment: Using the basic transform tools and keyboard shortcuts reduces friction when positioning and orienting assets. The Move tool lets you translate objects along axes; the Rotate tool changes orientation; the Scale tool adjusts size. Common shortcuts are Q for Hand, W for Move, E for Rotate, and R for Scale. Switching quickly between these tools keeps your hands on the keyboard and your eyes on the art. A practical example: when placing a decal, press W to nudge it into place, E to rotate it to match edges, and R to size it proportionally. Another useful set of shortcuts includes F to focus on a selection, and holding the spacebar plus mouse to pan in some systems. A misconception is thinking one tool is enough; in practice, switching between move and rotate is essential for fine placement. Also learn soft-snapping and numeric input fields in the Inspector when you require exact values. Practice a short routine: select an object, press F, use W to position, E to rotate, and R to scale until the element reads correctly in Game view. The main benefit is speed—these shortcuts let you iterate visually without interrupting your creative flow.

Shortcut list

  • W — Move tool (translate along axes)
  • E — Rotate tool (orient object)

Example workflow

When aligning a decorative object, focus with F, nudge position with W, correct rotation with E, and scale to fit with R. Use snap and numeric fields for precise alignment when needed.

Common mistake
Trying to get pixel-perfect alignment by dragging alone; instead use focus and numeric input when precision is required.
Pro tip
Learn a short keyboard routine for frequent tasks so your hands rarely leave the keyboard.

screens.title: Import Settings and Model Adjustments
screens.narratorSegment: When you import a model into the Project window, the Inspector exposes import settings that directly affect how that asset behaves in the scene. Key settings for artists include Import Scale, which ensures models match your scene units; Normals and Tangents that affect shading; and Mesh Compression which trades memory for fidelity. For textures, settings such as Max Size and Compression determine visual quality and runtime cost. A concrete example: if a car model imports too large, change Import Scale until the car matches a human-scale prop; then check normals to ensure lighting behaves correctly. A common mistake is leaving default import scales and later trying to rescale instances manually in the scene, which can break rigging or linked animations. Another pitfall is ignoring texture compression, which can cause memory issues on target platforms. Best practice is to set reasonable defaults at import, test in Game view, and document your chosen scale and compression standards. The takeaway: import settings are the first, crucial step to get assets into the scene with reliable scale and shading; adjust them early rather than compensating later in the scene.

Import settings to check
  • Scale Factor / Import Scale — match scene units early.
  • Normals & Tangents — control shading and normal mapping behavior.
  • Mesh Compression & Read/Write Flags — balance memory vs fidelity.
  • Texture Max Size & Compression — manage visual quality and runtime cost.
Key Takeaway

Fix scale and shading at import so assets behave predictably and avoid later fixes that break links or animations.

Practical example

Import a prop and adjust Import Scale until it aligns with a 1.8 meter character model. Then inspect normals and assign material to verify shading under scene lights in Game view.

Common mistake
Rescaling instances in the scene instead of changing the import scale, which can break animation scales or prefab references.
Pro tip
Document import scale and texture compression standards in a team README to keep assets consistent.

Welcome. In this lesson we’ll make the Unity Editor feel like your studio. You will learn what each core window does, how to move confidently through a 3D scene, and how to arrange the workspace so your art work stays visible and accessible. Artists use the Scene view to place and polish assets, the Game view to check the player’s perspective, the Hierarchy to structure scene objects, the Project window to manage files, and the Inspector to tune properties. I’ll show concrete navigation habits—like orbiting, panning, and using keyboard movement bindings—that save time while modeling and composing. We’ll also practice creating and saving an artist layout so you never lose a comfortable setup. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes—like dumping imports in the project root or ignoring import scale—that lead to confusion later. By the end, you’ll know which window to reach for when you want to reposition a prop, verify materials, or change a texture import setting. Think of this session as building a dependable studio workflow: small navigation habits and a tidy project structure translate to faster iterations and clearer visuals. Ready to set up your artist workspace?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify core editor windows, move efficiently through a 3D scene, create a custom artist layout, and use keyboard shortcuts that speed selection and manipulation. First, you’ll learn to recognize and describe the purpose of the Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector windows so you can pick the right tool for a task. Second, you’ll practice the fundamental navigation operations—panning, zooming, orbiting, and the fly controls—so moving through large scenes becomes quick and precise. Third, you’ll customize and save a layout tailored to visual work, which reduces the time spent resizing and redocking panels. Fourth, you’ll learn common keyboard shortcuts that let you switch between move, rotate, and scale tools and focus on selected objects. Each objective includes a short practice or micro-check to ensure you can perform the action, and you’ll be asked to reflect on a layout that supports your personal pipeline. These skills matter because they reduce context switching, limit errors during importing and placement, and keep your focus on lighting, composition, and material adjustments rather than hunting for windows.

These objectives are written to be demonstrable. You should be able to point to a window and state its purpose, perform a set of navigation maneuvers in the Scene view, and adjust import or material properties in the Inspector. For example, after practice you’ll import an FBX model, select it in the Project window, and change its import scale and orientation in the Inspector. You should also be able to select a Directional Light in the Hierarchy, focus it, orbit around it, and confirm how shadows behave in the Game view. Another objective is to create a simple folder structure, move assets into the correct folders, and explain why consistent naming matters for collaboration. Finally, you’ll save a custom layout and recall it on a new project. These are not abstract skills: they are the everyday operations that keep your visual pipeline fast, reproducible, and easy to share with other artists or engineers.

The Scene view is the interactive 3D viewport where you arrange and polish your assets. As an artist, you’ll spend the majority of your time here aligning models, placing lights, and previewing materials under scene lighting. Define it as your virtual studio: you can select objects, move them, change their parents, and preview how transformations affect the whole composition. A common practice is to orbit and pan frequently while modeling so you can inspect silhouettes and proportions from multiple angles. For example, select a small vase, press F to focus, then orbit while checking the rim for shading issues. A frequent misconception is that the Game view and Scene view are identical; they are not. Scene view offers editing controls, gizmos, and scene overlays that the Game view hides. Another mistake is relying only on mouse wheel zoom—mixing fly keys with right-button movement gives more precise camera placement in large scenes. Try this: pick a light, focus on it, move around using right-click plus WASD for smooth camera flight, and adjust the light until reflections look correct on a nearby model. The takeaway: make Scene view navigation habitual and precise, because fast, controlled viewing prevents small modeling errors from becoming big problems later.

Good camera control in the Scene view is a set of small, repeatable actions. Start with pan: hold the middle mouse button and drag to translate the view parallel to the screen—this is useful when lining up elements without changing perspective. Zoom with the scroll wheel for coarse distance changes; for precision, use focus on an object and then orbit. Orbiting is done with the right mouse button and mouse movement; it rotates the camera around the pivot point. A common, powerful technique is to combine right-button orbit with WASD and Q/E keys: this gives you a smooth fly-through camera that’s invaluable in larger environments where single-click pans feel imprecise. For example, when placing streetlamps across a scene, focus the first lamp, orbit to set angle, then fly forward with W and fine-tune with middle-mouse pans. A misconception is that faster camera movement always speeds work; it can make you miss alignment errors. Practice slow orbits when checking normals or material seams. Finally, learn the F key to focus objects and re-center your pivot. This saves time when scaling or rotating small props and ensures the gizmo handles behave predictably. Try a quick drill: focus, orbit, pan, zoom, and repeat until each movement feels natural and deliberate.

The Game view renders exactly what the player will see, based on the active camera in your scene. For an artist, it is the critical feedback loop: you make changes in the Scene view and verify them in the Game view to confirm composition, camera framing, and material appearance in play conditions. Unlike Scene view, the Game view hides editing gizmos and overlays, and it uses the camera’s projection, resolution, and post-processing settings. For example, your model may look correctly lit in Scene view, but in Game view the camera’s exposure or post-process bloom could alter highlights and color saturation. A common misconception is treating the Game view as purely for programmers; artists must use it to ensure that trims, specular highlights, and camera-driven effects work at the intended resolution. Try this concrete check: set the Game view resolution to the target device, run the Scene view changes, and compare. If a texture looks too shiny in Game view, inspect the material’s Smoothness and Metallic values in the Inspector; the Game view is your final arbiter for how the player will perceive your art. Ultimately, switching frequently between Scene and Game view keeps visual intent aligned with final presentation.

The Hierarchy window lists every GameObject in the active scene and displays parent-child relationships. For artists, using parenting deliberately simplifies complex transformations: moving a parent moves all its children, which is useful for grouped props like a character and its accessories. Define parenting as a way to lock multiple pieces to a single transform operation. For example, a street lamp assembly might have separate child objects for pole, lamp head, and bulb; rotating the pole should keep the lamp head and bulb attached. A common mistake is parenting meshes to each other without considering pivot placement—if the parent's pivot is far from the visible geometry, rotation and scale behavior can become awkward. Use empty GameObjects as organizational parents to provide predictable pivot points. Also keep the Hierarchy tidy: name objects descriptively and use folders or empty containers to group related items. This helps collaboration since other artists or engineers can understand intent at a glance. After organizing, practice: create a parent container, move a group into it, and then move the parent—observe how child transforms follow. The takeaway: good hierarchy design reduces errors and saves time when you need to move or duplicate complex assemblies.

The Project window is your asset library: it contains models, textures, materials, and any file in the Unity project. For an artist, a well-organized Project window is essential to maintain speed and avoid duplication. Use clear top-level folders like Models, Textures, Materials, and Scenes. When importing, place assets into the correct folder immediately rather than dumping them in the root. A common mistake is inconsistent naming—different artists might import the same prop under slightly different names and create redundant files. For example, import a rock model into Models/Rocks/LowPoly and place its texture in Textures/Rocks; then create a Material in Materials/Rocks that references those textures. This predictable layout makes it easy to find and reuse assets across scenes. Another practical habit is to use subfolders for LODs, variations, and source files. Finally, remember that moving assets in the Project window can break references if done carelessly; use Unity's move operations rather than moving files outside the editor.
